cards.q: Which of these hide an O(n) loop inside a loop body: `x in my_list`, `lst.pop(0)`, `lst.insert(0, x)`, `a[1:]`?
cards.a: All four. `in` on a list scans, `pop(0)` and `insert(0, x)` shift every item, and slicing copies. Price every line inside the loop, or one visible loop turns into O(n²).

cards.q: What does amortised O(1) mean for `list.append`, and how does it differ from average-case O(1)?
cards.a: Amortised is a guarantee over any sequence of operations: rare O(n) resizes average out to O(1) each, whatever the data. Average-case (a hash lookup) assumes friendly inputs.

cards.q: In two-sum with a dictionary, why must you check `target - x` before storing `seen[x] = i`?
cards.a: Otherwise a value finds itself: for `[3, 4]` and target 6 you return `[0, 0]`. Check the complement first, then store the current value.

cards.q: When counting subarrays with sum k using a dictionary, why must it start as `{0: 1}`?
cards.a: The empty prefix lets subarrays that start at index 0 be counted. Without it, `[1, 2]` with k = 3 returns 0 instead of 1. Look up before recording.

cards.q: Why use `while l < r`, not `l <= r`, in an opposite-end pair search on a sorted array?
cards.a: With `<=` the pointers can meet on one element and pair it with itself: `[5]` with target 10 would wrongly 'succeed'. A pair needs two different positions.

cards.q: Why does a shrinking sliding window fail for 'subarray sum equals k' when the array has negative numbers?
cards.a: A window needs a monotone rule: growing must never decrease the measure. With negatives the sum can fall again, so shrink logic breaks. Use prefix sums with a dictionary.

cards.q: Why is always choosing the last item as the pivot dangerous in quick sort, and what is the fix?
cards.a: On sorted input every split is lopsided: O(n²) time (500 items cost 124,750 comparisons) and deep recursion. Use a random pivot or median of three.

cards.q: A binary search uses `while lo < hi` with `hi = mid - 1`. What is wrong with it?
cards.a: It mixes a half-open loop with closed moves, so searching 5 in `[5]` never enters the loop. Pick one template: `lo <= hi` with `mid ± 1`, or `lo < hi` with `hi = mid`.

cards.q: When does binary search on the answer apply, and why round up with `(lo + hi + 1) // 2`?
cards.a: When a yes/no test on a value flips once as the value grows. Round up whenever a branch sets `lo = mid`; otherwise with `hi = lo + 1` the loop never ends.

cards.q: In iterative list reversal, what must you save before `cur.next = prev`, and what do you return?
cards.a: Save `nxt = cur.next` first, or the rest of the list is lost. Return `prev`, not `head`: the old head is now the tail.

cards.q: Why must a fast and slow pointer loop test `while fast and fast.next`, in that order?
cards.a: On even-length lists `fast` becomes `None`; on odd-length lists `fast.next` is `None`. Testing `fast` first avoids `AttributeError`. Compare nodes with `is`, not values.

cards.q: Why is a monotonic stack O(n) even with a `while` loop inside the `for` loop, and what do you store?
cards.a: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so total pops are at most n. Store indexes, not values, so you can compute distances and widths.

cards.q: In backtracking, why must you record `path[:]` (a copy) rather than `path`?
cards.a: `path` keeps changing, so `result` would hold the same list many times, all empty at the end. A copy freezes the answer at that moment.

cards.q: In combination sum, which index do you pass to the recursive call to allow reuse, and to forbid it?
cards.a: Pass `i` to allow reuse and `i + 1` for use once. Loop from `start`, not from 0, or you generate permutations such as both `[1,2]` and `[2,1]`.

cards.q: After sorting, which condition skips duplicates when generating unique subsets?
cards.a: Skip `nums[i]` when `i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]`. Using `i > 0` also skips valid deeper picks, so `[1, 2, 2]` disappears.

cards.q: Does tree 'height' count edges or nodes? Give the empty-tree and single-node values for each rule.
cards.a: Both are used, so state which. Edges: empty = -1, single node = 0. Nodes: empty = 0, single node = 1. 'Maximum depth' problems usually count nodes.

cards.q: Why is checking only `left < node < right` at each node not enough to validate a BST?
cards.a: The rule holds against all ancestors, not just the parent. Pass `(low, high)` bounds down the recursion so every node lies strictly between them.

cards.q: Why can `heappush(h, (node.val, node))` raise `TypeError`, and how do you fix it?
cards.a: When two values tie, Python compares the nodes, which are not comparable. Add a unique tie-breaker: `(node.val, i, node)`. Remember `heapq` is a min-heap.

cards.q: When should BFS mark a node visited: when pushed or when popped? Why?
cards.a: When pushed. Several neighbours can push the same node before its turn comes, so marking late queues it many times and can blow up the running time.

cards.q: How do you detect a cycle with Kahn's topological sort?
cards.a: Check that the order contains all n nodes. If a cycle exists, Kahn stops early and returns a shorter list, so test `len(order) == n`.

cards.q: Why compare `find(a) == find(b)` rather than `parent[a] == parent[b]` in union-find?
cards.a: `parent` is only the direct parent, not the leader, so two nodes in one group can differ. Always compare roots. Path compression plus union by rank make `find` nearly O(1).

cards.q: Why does Dijkstra break with a negative edge? Give a failing example.
cards.a: A node is declared final too early. With 0→1 cost 2, 0→2 cost 5 and 2→1 cost -4, the true distance to 1 is 1, but Dijkstra reports 2.

cards.q: Why is `return dp[-1]` wrong for longest increasing subsequence, and what is right?
cards.a: `dp[i]` is the best chain ending at i, which can end anywhere. For `[1, 2, 3, 0]` the last cell is 1 but the answer is 3. Return `max(dp)`.

cards.q: In 1D knapsack, which capacity direction do you scan for 0/1 versus unbounded?
cards.a: 0/1 knapsack and subset sum scan capacity downward so each item is used once. Unbounded knapsack and coin change scan upward so items can repeat. Mnemonic: backward means once.

cards.q: Why does 'take the biggest coin' fail for coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, and what proves a greedy rule?
cards.a: Greedy gives 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins) but 3 + 3 needs 2. Examples never prove greedy; an exchange argument does, or DP when you can break it.

cards.q: To keep the most non-overlapping intervals, what do you sort by, and why not by start time?
cards.a: Sort by end time. On `[1,10], [2,3], [4,5], [6,7]`, sorting by start keeps only `[1,10]` (1 interval); sorting by end keeps 3.

cards.q: In Python, what does `1 << n - 1` mean, and how do you build a mask of n ones?
cards.a: `+` and `-` bind tighter than `<<`, so it means `1 << (n - 1)`. Use `(1 << n) - 1`. Also `~x` equals `-x - 1`.

cards.q: In an LRU cache, what must every successful `get` do, and what must eviction delete?
cards.a: A `get` (and every `put` of an existing key) moves the key to newest. Eviction removes the oldest node from the list and its key from the map, keeping both in sync.

cards.q: In a queue built from two stacks, when do you pour the inbox into the outbox?
cards.a: Only when the outbox is empty. Pouring on every pop puts newer items on top and returns the wrong item. Each item moves once, so pops are O(1) amortised.

cards.q: Why is 'one loop, so O(n)' a wrong claim when the body calls `list.index`?
cards.a: `index`, `in list` and slices cost O(n) each, so the loop is O(n²). Count what happens inside the loop, not only the loop itself.

quiz.q: What does this print? `g = [[0] * 3] * 2; g[0][0] = 1; print(g)`
quiz.why: The outer `*` repeats a reference to one inner list, so both rows are the same object. Build rows separately with a comprehension: `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]`.

quiz.q: Two-sum code stores `seen[x] = i` before checking `target - x`. For `[3, 4]` and target 6, what does it return?
quiz.why: The first value 3 is stored, then `6 - 3 = 3` is found in `seen`, so index 0 pairs with itself. Check the complement first, then store.

quiz.q: For a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], the padded prefix array is P = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14]. What is the sum of a[1..3] inclusive?
quiz.why: `P[4] - P[1] = 9 - 3 = 6` (1 + 4 + 1). `P[3] - P[1] = 5` forgets `a[3]`, the classic off-by-one.

quiz.q: What does this print? `data = [3, 1, 2]; result = data.sort(); print(result)`
quiz.why: `list.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`. Use `sorted(data)` when you need a new sorted list.

quiz.q: Weights 1 to 10 must ship in 5 days in order, each day carrying at most the capacity. What is the minimum capacity?
quiz.why: Binary search the capacity between 10 (the heaviest package) and 55. At 14 you need 6 days; at 15 the packages fit in 5 days. 10 is only the lower bound.

quiz.q: A list 1→2→3→4→5 is walked with `slow` moving 1 step and `fast` moving 2 steps while `fast and fast.next`. Where does `slow` stop?
quiz.why: `fast` ends on node 5 when `slow` has taken 2 steps, so `slow` is on node 3, the middle. For even lengths it lands on the second middle node.

quiz.q: Daily temperatures [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]. Using a monotonic stack of indexes, what are the days to wait for a warmer day?
quiz.why: Day 2 (75) waits 4 days for 76. Each popped index gets `i - popped`. The first option is the next-smaller variant, and the last two are off-by-one slips.

quiz.q: A subsets backtracker for [1, 2] pushes and pops a shared `path`, but records `result.append(path)` without a copy. What is `result` at the end?
quiz.why: All four entries are the same list object, and after all `pop` calls it is empty. Recording `path[:]` gives the four real subsets.

quiz.q: What happens when you call `f(5)` with `def f(n): return n * f(n - 1)`?
quiz.why: There is no base case, so the recursion never ends and Python stops it at its default depth limit. A base case such as `if n <= 1: return 1` fixes it.

quiz.q: After `heappush` of 5, then 1, then 3 into an empty list `h`, what does `print(h)` show?
quiz.why: A heap only guarantees the smallest item at index 0. The rest follows the heap shape, not sorted order. Pop repeatedly to get sorted values.

quiz.q: Which traversal prints the values of a binary search tree in sorted order?
quiz.why: Inorder visits left subtree, node, then right subtree, and in a BST everything on the left is smaller. Preorder and postorder follow the shape, not the order of values.

quiz.q: Edges 0→1 (cost 2), 0→2 (cost 5), 2→1 (cost -4). Standard Dijkstra settles each node once. What does it report for node 1, and what is the true distance?
quiz.why: Node 1 is settled at cost 2 before the cheaper route 0→2→1 (5 - 4 = 1) is seen. Negative weights break Dijkstra. Use Bellman-Ford.

quiz.q: A graph has 6 nodes (0 to 5) and edges (0,1), (1,2), (3,4). How many connected components does it have?
quiz.why: The groups are {0,1,2}, {3,4} and the isolated node {5}. Forgetting isolated nodes gives 2.

quiz.q: `dp[i]` is the longest increasing chain ending at index i. For [1, 2, 3, 0], which expression gives the answer?
quiz.why: The best chain can end anywhere, so take the maximum. The last cell is 1 here because the chain ending at 0 has length 1.

quiz.q: Coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6. How many coins does 'biggest first' greedy use, and how many does the optimum use?
quiz.why: Greedy takes 4 first and needs 1 + 1 afterwards. DP finds 3 + 3. Greedy works for 1, 5, 10, 25 but not for every coin system.

quiz.q: For n = 0, 6 and 8, which values does `(n & (n - 1)) == 0` accept?
quiz.why: `8 & 7 = 0` and `0 & -1 = 0` pass, while `6 & 5 = 4` fails. The power-of-two test needs `n > 0` to reject 0.

quiz.q: An LRU cache has capacity 2. You run put(1), put(2), get(1), put(3). Which key is evicted?
quiz.why: The `get(1)` makes key 1 the newest, so key 2 is least recently used and leaves when put(3) overflows. Without refreshing on `get`, key 1 would be wrongly evicted.

quiz.q: Which pattern fits 'longest substring without repeating characters'?
opts: Variable-size sliding window with a last-seen map
Two pointers on a sorted array
quiz.why: The right end grows each step and the left end jumps only past a repeat inside the window (`last[ch] >= left`). Prefix sums and sorting do not apply to this rule.
